Grid Structure

cuDisc uses a structured 2D mesh in the poloidal plane of an axisymmetric protoplanetary disc. The coordinate system is cylindrical radius R and polar angle θ measured from the midplane, so θ = 0 corresponds to the disc equatorial plane and increasing θ approaches the disc surface.

Coordinate system

Cell interfaces are surfaces of constant R (cylinders) and constant θ (cones). The cell (i, j) is bounded by radii Re,i and Re,i+1, and by polar angles θe,j and θe,j+1. In cylindrical coordinates (R, Z), the Z-faces are therefore not flat planes but tilted surfaces.

Note

This grid is a non-orthogonal quadrilateral mesh. The radial and vertical directions are not perpendicular to each other in the (R, Z) plane. The consequence is that the face normals in the Z-direction have a non-zero component in R.

Cell volumes and face areas

The volume of cell (i, j) is (Robinson et al. 2024, Eq. 1):

\[V_{ij} = \frac{1}{3}\,\Delta(R^3)_i\,\Delta(\tan\theta)_j\]

where \(\Delta(R^3)_i = R_{e,i+1}^3 - R_{e,i}^3\) and \(\Delta(\tan\theta)_j = \tan\theta_{e,j+1} - \tan\theta_{e,j}\). The factor of 1/3 follows from integrating over the azimuthal angle and the volume element \(R\,\mathrm{d}R\,\mathrm{d}Z\).

The face area in the R-direction (between cells (i−1, j) and (i, j)) is (Eq. 2):

\[A^R_{ij} = R_{e,i}^2\,\Delta(\tan\theta)_j\]

The face area in the Z-direction (between cells (i, j−1) and (i, j)) is (Eq. 3):

\[A^Z_{ij} = \frac{R_{e,i+1}^3 - R_{e,i}^3}{3\,R_{c,i}}\, \frac{1}{\cos\theta_{e,j}}\]

These forms are chosen to avoid numerical cancellation as R → 0.

Face normals

The outward normal to the R-face pointing from cell (i−1, j) into cell (i, j) is simply \(\hat{n}^R = (1, 0)\) in cylindrical coordinates.

The outward normal to the Z-face pointing from cell (i, j−1) into cell (i, j) is

\[\hat{n}^Z = \bigl(-\sin\theta_{e,j},\;\cos\theta_{e,j}\bigr)\]

reflecting the tilted nature of the constant-θ faces.

Grid spacing

Radial grid spacing

The standard choice for disc simulations is logarithmic spacing, so that cells have constant fractional width \(\Delta R / R\). This is set by RadialSpacing::log in the grid parameters.

For cases where higher resolution is needed at large radii, power-law spacing with \(\Delta R \propto R^{p_R}\) is available via RadialSpacing::power and the parameter R_power.

Polar-angle grid spacing

The polar grid must resolve both the optically thin surface layers (which require fine angular resolution near θ = 0) and the optically thick midplane regions (which require cells that span a sufficient vertical column). The subdivided grid (ThetaSpacing::subdiv) satisfies both requirements:

  • From θ = 0 to theta_subdiv, cells are uniformly spaced.

  • From theta_subdiv to θmax, cells follow a power law with exponent theta_power.

A typical choice is theta_subdiv = π/9 (20°) and theta_power = 0.75, which concentrates cells in the disc atmosphere while still covering the midplane.

Ghost cells

Two layers of ghost cells surround the active domain on each side (set by Nghost = 2 in the grid parameters). Ghost cells are used exclusively to implement boundary conditions; physical quantities are never evolved in them directly. The solvers fill ghost cells at the start of each time step according to the chosen boundary condition flags.

Boundary conditions

Boundaries are specified per edge using flags from BoundaryFlags:

Edge

Default in examples

Inner radial (Rmin)

Outflow (open_R_inner)

Outer radial (Rmax)

Outflow (open_R_outer)

Lower polar (θ = 0, midplane)

Closed/reflecting (midplane symmetry)

Upper polar (θmax)

Outflow (open_Z_outer)

The midplane is always treated as a symmetry plane; no flag is needed for it.
